tags.gist: Says the paper asks the right questions but frames a product question; the real question is what clinical authority a system has earned and keeps.
Recommends adapting clinician licensure into nine stages from competency examination through supervised deployment, provisional and independent authorization, monitoring and revalidation.
Wants the framework never to make a system that beats the human standard of care harder to deploy than the care it replaces.
Rests on four principles: risk by consequence and agency, competency by benchmarking and confirmation, autonomy earned not assumed, and authorization maintained by continuous evidence.
Extends published licensure proposals with a numeric threshold for independent deployment, an agentic autonomy ladder and tiered change regulation.
Wants five risk axes instead of two: consequence, clinical agency, reversibility, time to harm and human recoverability, with evidence rising with agency.
Wants FDA to judge the authority an output actually exercises through specificity, personalization, urgency, ranking and omitted alternatives, not the feature label.
Says patient-facing AI is not automatically higher risk; evaluate literacy fit, uncertainty communication, emergency recognition and false reassurance, scaling burden to consequence.
Wants the comparator set prospectively from the clinical task and its environment, not from whether the user is a generalist or specialist.
Wants realistic trajectories tested, including escalation, contradiction, user pressure and prompt injection, since intended use spans every role a conversation can assume.
Wants sponsors to define context-specific costs for each error direction before approval and optimize both, rather than one blended metric.
Calls benchmarking then confirmation directionally right but only the front end of a nine-stage pipeline where competence is never assumed permanent.
Would let low-risk informational functions rely on benchmarking and human factors while high-risk autonomous ones add shadow deployment, prospective and team evaluation.
Would add scope discipline, clinical humility, longitudinal consistency and human-AI team performance to the competency domains.
Wants three evidence layers, public benchmarks, sequestered regulatory benchmarks and real-world confirmation, with none sufficient alone for high-risk AI.
Would formalize five confirmation tiers from retrospective through shadow, supervised and controlled autonomous deployment, climbed in order with the tier set by risk.
Wants both statistical and clinical significance, with prespecified meaningful effect sizes and allowance for rare-event settings.
Would let synthetic data expand the test universe but never become the evidence, favoring independently generated and validated datasets for consequential decisions.
Says there is no universal comparator: an autonomous function should be compared with the care pathway it actually replaces, even no intervention until morning rounds.
Wants an assistive tool judged as the human-AI team against the clinician alone, since value does not require beating the best clinician.
Wants an FDA-overseen network of multiple third parties built on ASCA and MDDT, with transparent accreditation, conflict rules and appeals, never a single gatekeeper.
Agrees competency rules apply across architectures, since every model should face the same questions about function, inputs, authority and failure.
Accepts the trade for low and moderate-risk reversible functions with real-time monitoring, but not as a substitute for high-consequence autonomous ones.
Proposes a continuous clinical license with scheduled, event-triggered and signal-triggered reassessment running in parallel.
Says a supervisory AI needs its own benchmark, independent validation and audit trail, functioning like a clinical monitoring system for high-risk uses.
Assigns distinct roles to manufacturer, institution, clinician, model provider, society, evaluator and FDA, with the manufacturer primarily accountable.
Proposes minor, material and major modification tiers sorted by clinical behavior change rather than code size or version number.
Wants a PCCP to define the fence, authorized behavior, required performance, uncrossable boundaries and revalidation triggers, rather than predict each change.
Wants version identification, advance notice, rollback and audit logs so a changed foundation model cannot be a liability shield.
Finds voluntary master files insufficient for the highest-risk systems and would pair them with contractual disclosure duties and FDA authority to request more.
Proposes a five-level clinical agency ladder from information to autonomous practice, with evidence demands rising steeply at each level.
Integrates everything into a Clinical AI License with eight elements and nine stages, where scope can expand with performance or be restricted on degradation.
Proposes a falsifiable threshold: provisional authorization at half the specialty clinician baseline under supervision, independent authorization at full parity.
Flags state medical boards' objection to licensing AI and asks FDA to say whether it will only authorize autonomy or expect boards to reconcile.
Lists twelve recommendations, including regulating capability not architecture, graduated earned autonomy, dynamic authorization and rewarding superior outcomes.
Agrees FDA is right that conventional testing may not suffice and right to explore competency evaluation, confirmation, monitoring and agentic approaches.
Urges regulating AI according to the authority it has been granted, adapting the established system for managing clinician competence under uncertainty.
